review_text_raw:
I want to like this game, but there are some frustrating design flaws that detract from what should be a fun hacklite game. I kept running into the same issues time and again throughout the campaign, here are a couple of examples.

- There are some storylines that require you to play perfectly to proceed. Failure can lock you out from retrying, and many times the way forward is very obtuse. For example, in one mission you must stop an assassin from boarding a train. To unmask the assassin in the first place you must have played efficiently enough in previous missions, to have had enough spare time left to investigate several non-objective data nodes. Then you have to figure out that one of the terms in an email can be searched for on the In[T]ranet, and then recall information from over a dozen missions earlier. In this mission you must now disrupt the track to delay the train, without affecting any other tracks, which also means failure. First you have to be inquisitive enough (and have enough trace time to) investigate a non-objective data node and find out that the target train has been rescheduled from track C to Track B. Upon sabotaging track B you get an update showing that the objective to stop the assassin from boarding was successful! Mission complete right? Well apparently not. Disconnecting at this stage gives you a blank mission summary and prevents you from reattempting the mission. As much as I want to know what went wrong I'm not willing to start the game from the beginning to try and find out.

- The RNG can really mess you up. This one is pretty simple, you need to use a stealth program to avoid the trace bar filling up. Instead of being based on turns or measured progress, it's a % chance to increase every turn. This means that sometimes running restrictive heavy stealth can fail you several times in a row, or sometimes token measures will prevent a trace for many turns in a row. Some missions have very low trace bars, meaning a bit of bad RNG can cause you to fail. Running into (randomly placed) ICE also increases trace, and you are forced to either waste time scanning for it or run into it headlong. There are many other examples of RNG messing up your timing or causing undue grief.

- The game throws a lot of unexpected curveballs and suckerpunches at you. This is made worse by the fact that you can only carry (by default) 5 programs with you on each mission.  Sure the portscanner on the mission selection screen will generally give you broad sense of what you might be facing, but the specifics really do matter. What if you pick hive (an attack program that is very weak at the start of the mission but becomes more powerful as you infect more nodes) and a wall ICE spawns between the access node and the rest of the network? Suddenly you spend half the trace bar just breaking through the first obstacle, leaving no time for the mission objectives. There's also a poorly pre-informed boss battle where the boss ICE/AI may randomly destroy one of your software packages. Yes, you can hack a specific node to disable this attack, but RNG decided that he would use it immediately on me and remove my only breaker app (ie I'm now unarmed against a boss). The game really likes throwing these kinds of scenarios at you out of left field, and failure usually means you can't re-attempt the mission without starting a new game.

- The Morality Penalty. Simply put, blackhat actions reward you grossly while whitehat actions leave you starving for resources. In many cases the whitehat missions available have no payout or even ask you to spend credits on the mission itself. Some of the better attack programs are also locked behind blackhat rank, while whitehat will give you an extra defensive option or two (sitting still spamming defensive measures is not great, a lot of missions have timers).

All in all, many of these could have been alleviated if there wasn't such a reliance on RNG or bringing the perfect combination of apps. As it is, many missions feel more like a gamble than proper foresight or strategy.

review_text_raw:
The use of a turn based mechanic is interesting, as most of the 'hacking' games usually rely on speed - and it could have led to an interesting strategy-ish game.
Unfortunately, the heavy use of RNG is infuriating (and you can see from tests & other comments that it doesn't get better as you progress) - contrary to pretty much the rest of the niche of 'hacking' games, which is about skill (sometimes unforgiving and frustrating, but about skill and/or speed nonetheless), MP seems to have chosen a luck and "die and retry" approach. This makes the defeats frustrating and the victories devoid of any satisfaction.

review_text_raw:
An interesting concept. With all the interesting programs you can add to your deck, this should have been a solid turn-based strategy/puzzle game, but it's so restrictive and RNG-based from the start that it can easily turn into a "try, die, repeat until you get lucky" experience. After my sixth time restarting a single mission because of bad luck rather than lack of skill (getting a trace+ three times in a row despite having cloak at 75%, SysOps making a beeline for me at exactly the wrong moment, etc.), I realized I wasn't having fun anymore, so I turned it off and sorted it into my "not worth it" pile.

It's a shame, because there was a lot of potential to love here and it would have been right up my alley if the RNG was a little more forgiving.

EDIT: Devs have pointed out that there ARE difficulty settings. It took me a bit to find them, but they do exist, so I've edited the review to reflect that and to add examples for the bad luck I had.

The core seems like it could be fun, but the frustrations detract too much.

review_text_raw:
The game is a novel concept, but I have to unfortunately call a spade a spade here.

This game is a turn-based hacking game with RNG elements that make the game severely unfun. They also got some very clear inspiration from Hacknet with the main characters name being literally taken from the character from Hacknet, Data. There's also Clover, another homage to Hacknet (I believe). They even have a port command, except instead of PortHack it's PortSeek/PortSeeker.

Unfortunately I simply can't recommend this game. The fact that it's turn-based is fine, but the RNG element really just throws it under the water. If you want a hacking game, get Hacknet.

review_text_raw:
Midnight Protocol is a desktop/hacking sim, and like all of these games, has nothing to do with actual hacking and is utterly unrealistic.  So this is just a strategy (turn based or realtime, you choose) game where you plug away controlling nodes or whatever.  The game does work but it's needlessly convoluted.  I guess to illustrate this, it takes 1/10th the time to learn how to play an RTS like Command & Conquer for 10x the rewarding gameplay.  And even though it's only a 2D game, C&C also has better graphics than this. 

The game design is somewhat flawed in some ways, with a reliance on procgen and RNG that can make or break each challenge. But mostly the game falls flat hard on a very weak and amateurish technical and visual presentation, and sloppy, and in some ways offensive interface design. 

On the upside, the game does feature customisable controls and resolution, so at least some of the basic, minimum requirements have been met.  Unfortunately there's a number of other technical defects and shortcomings which contribute to the game being difficult to recommend to gamers.

The game features lazy minimalist/untextured low-polygon "retro" assets and visuals, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the early 1990s.  The lack of textures is a method that lazy devs often use to disguise their lack of talent/interest in doing the graphics properly and trying to disguise it under the name of "art", or "We made it look bad on purpose", which really isn't something gamers should have to put up with.  It's unclear why the developers weren't willing to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets and high resolution textures for the game.  It looks bad as a result of their decisions, and that's just another reason to avoid it.

To make matters worse, there's no mouse input, despite this being sold on PC as if it were a PC game.  This is unacceptable and somewhat insulting.  I know this is on purpose to make it seem like some kind of cool "hacker" game but this is annoying. Don't do this.  No developer should ever dictate to gamers how a game is to be played, ever. 

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

Midnight Protocol didn't appeal much to the people who own a copy of the game, either.  It has achievements, and they show us a very clear picture that the game didn't really capture any interest from gamers.  The most commonly and easily attained achievement is for finishing the tutorial, trivial to get, but less than 39 percent of players bothered to get that far before uninstalling the game.  Hardly a success story, gamers just weren't all that interested in the game.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?

Midnight Protocol has the laughable, eye-watering price of $15 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.

For comparison, the $15 asking price for this game could get you games like "Mass Effect Andromeda", "Project Zomboid" or "Stellaris".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.

[b]My reviews for other games have no bearing on the dismal quality of this failed product[/b].

Nothing in the developers pointless breach of Valve guidelines changes any of the objective facts of my review.  My review stands unaltered.  I cannot recommend this game to anyone.

review_text_raw:
Let's start with the positives. The visuals are very good, very "hackery" and just very pleasing to look at. It's also keyboard only, which further enhances the immersion.

And this is about it when it comes to the positives.

It's almost fundamentally not a hacking game. You could easily swap out all of the "commands" for just fantasy spells. You're not breaking into systems to gather information, to gather passwords to use on other networks (i.e. puzzle solving). Each "mission" is fundamentally independent. You're there to get money (or complete objectives for the story) and then leave.

There's also the weird RNG aspect of the game. Your "attacks" against "firewalls" can "crit". Not to mention, how many actions waste your action points, which is also complemented by how few turns you actually from being caught.

The developer has a solid foundation to creating an interesting hacking game. But if they're going to do a RNG/RPG turn-based game, then stick to fantasy/sci-fi instead.
